speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Before that Act, Coroner's Inquiries were dealt with under the Criminal Procedure Code.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The 2010 Act updated our coronial system to clarify its role and also, strengthen its procedures, so that it could better serve the public interest.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: First, the Coroner's Inquiry became fact-finding, rather than fault-finding.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Second, the Coroner was empowered to tap on the technical expertise of forensic pathologists or assessors, to facilitate more effective coronial investigations.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Third, it re-scoped the Coroner's jurisdiction, giving it a clearer focus.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This Act had served us well over the last decade.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Currently, section 12 of the Act requires the Coroner to view the body as soon as possible, in all cases, after a death is reported to him.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This is to ensure that the deceased is correctly identified.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: However, today, the viewing of the body by the Coroner may not be necessary in all cases in order to correctly identify the body.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We have other safeguards, which use technology to ensure the correct identification of bodies.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Today, when a death is reported to the Police, the following steps take place.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The Police Investigation Officer (IO) will investigate the deceased's identity at the scene by, for example, interviewing the next-of-kin, and also obtaining the deceased's NRIC or passport.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The Police IO will then record the deceased's particulars on a tag, which will be attached to the body at the scene.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: At the mortuary, the Police IO will present the deceased's NRIC or other identification documents to the Health Sciences Authority (HSA) staff for registration.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Two additional body tags will also be attached to the body in the mortuary: first, a Radio-Frequency Identification (RFID) tag to track the body's movement within the mortuary; and, two, a QR code body tag to confirm the deceased's identity.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: A Body Identification Form (BIF), which includes details such as the deceased's full name and NRIC number, will be generated upon registration.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: A photograph of the deceased's face and the body tags will also be taken and attached to the BIF.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The same Police IO, who recorded the deceased's particulars at the scene, will verify the accuracy of the BIF, before the BIF is sent to the Coroner.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The Coroner will then check the BIF against the report filed by the Police IO.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: These steps and safeguards are sufficient to ensure correct identification of the deceased.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Indeed, as far as we can tell, there have been so far no cases of misidentification since this set of protocols, processes and safeguards were put in place.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The Coroner will still be able to view the body if the Coroner considers this to be necessary.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: For example, the Coroner may wish to view the body in a case where foul play is suspected, or where the death may have wider implications on international relations.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In addition, the amendment will not affect the Coroner's duty to carry out a preliminary investigation into the cause of and circumstances connected with the death.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: During the preliminary investigation, the Coroner will consult the HSA forensic pathologist and the Police IO.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The Coroner will generally ask the Police IO about the scene investigations and any witness accounts.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Where the deceased's identity is unclear, the Coroner may then direct further steps, such as checking missing persons records, fingerprint identification and also forensic analysis, as may be appropriate.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The forensic pathologist will generally study the CT scan carried out on the body in the mortuary and the deceased's medical records, to determine the possible cause of death.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This is introduced by the new section 17A.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: It aims to deal with a situation where the deceased, firstly, had sustained an injury, contracted a disease or suffered a condition outside Singapore, that apparently caused the death; or, second, held certain positions in a foreign state, such as being a government minister; or was the spouse or child of persons holding certain positions in a foreign state.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In such situations, it is possible that a foreign state may request Singapore not to conduct a post-mortem examination on the body, so that the foreign state may itself carry out its own examination.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: At present, under the scope of our Act today, it is not possible to accede to such requests.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The Act requires the Coroner to certify the cause of death based on the findings of the Coroner's Inquiry – if one is held – or based on the available evidence if a Coroner's Inquiry is not held.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: However, there may be some cases where a post-mortem examination might be necessary to determine the cause of death, for example, if there are no external visible manifest signs of injury or disease.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In such cases, a post-mortem examination must be carried out before the Coroner can release the body.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In order for this to happen, three conditions must be fulfilled.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Alternatively, the Minister must be satisfied that the deceased had certain positions in the foreign state, such as being a government minister, or was the spouse or child of certain persons in such positions.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Third, the Minister must be satisfied, after having regard to the circumstances of the case and any undertaking given by the foreign state, that it is not in the public interest for the provisions of the Act to apply to the deceased.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In other words, the assessment is made as to whether there is a public interest, notwithstanding the request by the foreign state, for the examination to take place in Singapore.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In deciding whether to issue a certificate, the Minister may consider various factors, such as the forensic pathologist's views on the death; the Police's investigative findings on the death; the Public Prosecutor's views as to the likelihood of any criminal prosecutions in relation to the death and the likely impact of an exemption on such prosecutions.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: And fourthly, the purpose for which the request was made by the foreign state.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The Bill does not change the default position under the Act, which is that the Coroner will investigate deaths falling within the Coroner's jurisdiction.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: It is only in exceptional cases that the default position may be departed from under the new section 17A; and the three conditions I have mentioned above must be met and, in particular, I stress that the Minister must be satisfied that it would not be in our public interest for the usual coronial process to apply to the deceased.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I only have one area of clarification that I seek from the hon Minister.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Principally, the deaths that are proposed to be exempted from the Act are persons who died in Singapore, arising from conditions contracted outside Singapore or are for persons who are or were part of foreign government; this includes the spouse or child of the person too.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: My concern is how this proposal squares with the existing framework of the Coroners Act dealing with the Public Prosecutor's powers.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: When the hon Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs and Law, Prof Ho Peng Kee moved the Coroners Bill in 2010, he stated, as recounted by the hon Minister, that the Coroner's role is purely fact-finding.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It is not the job of the Coroner to decide who is criminally responsible for the death.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: He stressed that it is the Public Prosecutor who has the constitutional responsibility of who should be prosecuted for being responsible for the death.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: That was why the current Act provides for the Public Prosecutor to have wide-ranging powers, which includes the power to direct a Coroner to order a post-mortem examination, direct a forensic pathologist to investigate the cause of and circumstances connected with the death and direct a Coroner to hold an inquiry into any death occurring in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I am concerned about a situation where the Minister and the Public Prosecutor may not be ad idem on the issue of whether the death should be exempt from the Act.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This is the case in the Criminal Law (Temporary Provisions) Act (CLTPA).

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: As Members would know, the CLTPA may be invoked by the Minister to detain a person who is believed to have engaged in criminal acts affecting public safety, peace and good order.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In fact, it is expressly provided in the Act that nothing in that Act derogates from the powers of the Public Prosecutor with regard to the control and direction of criminal prosecutions.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I will be grateful for the hon Minister's explanation on this matter.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I have concerns about both provisions and would like the Ministry's clarifications.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: That is, when the Coroner is conducting his preliminary investigations into a reportable death, he can decide not to view the body at all.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: As for the rationale for this change, it was stated in the MinLaw release that this would "expedite the process of the body to the family and will also save resources for the Police, the Health Sciences Authority and the Coroner".

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: However, we must ask, to what extent will this change result in any compromise of investigations of deaths?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Despite what the Minister said earlier, it is not clear, to me at least, on what basis or the kinds of cases that are appropriate for a Coroner to decide that viewing of the body is not required.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Could the Minister please elaborate further on how the Coroner would be supported to ensure that he or she does not inadvertently miss or overlook important evidence that further investigations into the death may be warranted?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The second change brought about by this Bill is to give the Minister for Law the power to issue a certificate for the release of the body of a deceased person at the request of a foreign state.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: First, where the deceased had sustained an injury, contracted a disease or suffered a condition outside Singapore that appears to have caused the death; or, second, where the deceased person was or formerly was a head of state, head of government, government minister, government official or spouse or child of these persons or a diplomatic agent of a foreign state.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: A post-mortem should not be carried out and any Coroner's Inquiry into the death should cease.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: According to the media release by MinLaw on 13 September, one of the reasons is that the foreign state may wish to conduct its own post-mortem examination on the citizen or resident who happened to die in Singapore after sustaining an injury, contracting a disease or suffering a condition outside of Singapore.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I have two observations to make on this.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: First, it should be noted that the proposed section 17A phrases the conditions of (a)(i) and (a)(ii) as alternatives.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: So, for example, if the deceased happens to be an incumbent or a former head of government, it is not necessary that the deceased should have sustained an injury or illness outside of Singapore that appeared to lead to his death.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The deceased's very status as a current or former head of government is enough to bring up such a case within the new regime even if the cause of death has no overseas nexus.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This could be motivated by a desire to preserve the dignity of a formal leader, but could also be motivated by less noble reasons, for example, to cover up a death deliberately caused to a political opponent.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: We cannot dismiss this possibility and it is certainly not far-fetched that political adversaries could be killed through poisoning or other nefarious means.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The likelihood of the death of a foreign leader occurring in Singapore is not low as Singapore is a noted destination for medical treatment.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It goes without saying that when a death occurs in Singapore, important evidence surrounding the death may well be located in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Furthermore, such evidence may not be immediately available after the death as the Police may need time to uncover it.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Thus, there are risks associated with a quick handover of records and evidence to the foreign state.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: He can order investigations in Singapore to continue if he believes it to be in the public interest to do so.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: He can also subsequently revoke an earlier certificate for release.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: As a member of the international community, we have a part to play to ensure that history is accurately recorded and that the world is not misled by fake news about the death of national leaders and officials.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The Minister will need to be alive to this risk, even as he will likely face pressure from the requesting foreign state.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The Coroners Act came into effect in January 2011.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Was there any recent incident where a foreign state objected to or requested for exemption from the Coroner holding an inquiry?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: What were the difficult circumstances in that case, if at all, or those cases which prompted the Government to wish to give the Government the discretion not to hold such an inquiry?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I would also like to ask the Minister, in making such an amendment, whether the Government has done a study of the likely reciprocity from other countries based on their current laws.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I would also like to ask the Minister whether the proposed discretion is widely available in other countries.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: According to MinLaw, there are two reasons for the suggested change: (a) the viewing of the body serves "to ensure that the deceased is correctly identified.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: However, there are already existing safeguards to ensure the correct identification of bodies", which the Minister has touched on today; and (b) this will expedite the process of releasing the body to the family, and will also save resources for the Police, the Health Sciences Authority and the Coroner.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: In the debate to the Coroners’ Bill in 2010, the Senior Minister of State introducing the Bill, Assoc Prof Ho Peng Kee, said that: "…this provision will enable the Coroner to harness technology in appropriate cases, where the Coroner may be indisposed to be physically present to view the body, without having to cause unnecessary delay to the progress of time-sensitive investigations.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: This will expedite the release of the body to the next-of-kin after the Coroner has viewed and identified it.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: But let me assure Dr Lam that the norm will still be the current practice of the Coroner going down physically, right to the mortuary every morning to view and identify the body, and that includes weekends and public holidays." The Minister was replying to a Member Dr Lam Pin Min’s question and comment about whether letting the Coroner view and identify a body by video in lieu of viewing in-person, to decide whether an inquiry is needed, trivialises the investigative process.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Needless to say, viewing the body is an important step in determining whether a death happened due to natural causes or whether an inquiry into the cause of death is needed.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Comparing Assoc Prof Ho Peng Kee’s remarks on the default practice of the Coroner going down physically to the mortuary to view and identify the body, to the present proposed amendments, there appears to be a significant mindset shift on this.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: If not, what is the expectation of the Government with respect to when the Coroner is expected to attend in person?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: If so, will the Minister elaborate on this resource shortage?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: If "saving resources for the Police, the Health Sciences Authority and the Coroner" was a key consideration, would ramping up on resourcing be a more robust solution than making this key step a discretionary one?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This flexibility will save the valuable resources of the Coroner, Police, Health Sciences Authority and all other related parties.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: That said, I have three quick points of clarification.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My first point is on the Coroner’s investigation process.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Body viewing is one of the steps the Coroner must take in investigating and determining the cause and circumstances surrounding a reported death.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Having a proper procedure in place is important because it provides reassurance to the deceased’s family and similarly protects the Coroner from any allegations of wrongdoing or negligence.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: With the amendment to make such body viewing discretionary, can the Minister share what remaining mandatory requirements the Coroner has to fulfil in its preliminary investigation?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My second point is on the safeguards to ensure correct identification of bodies.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I note that existing safeguards to ensure the correct identification will remain.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: As Minister has shared, these safeguards include the tagging of the body with the deceased’s particulars at the scene and at the mortuary, the Police signing off on a Body Identification Form and sending it to the Coroner.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister share if additional steps will be taken to strengthen the existing safeguards to ensure correct identification notwithstanding the removal of the mandatory body viewing requirement?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My third point is on the revocation of certificates to release the bodies of deceased persons to foreign states.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Under the new section 17A(4), the Minister also has the power to revoke any Minister’s certificate previously issued.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister clarify under what circumstances would the Minister’s certificate be revoked?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Is there a time limit in exercising the revocation?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: If the certificate is revoked after the body has been buried, cremated, or transported out of the country, can the Minister share what methods and procedures are in place to ensure that the quality of the resumed investigation under the new section 17A(4)(a) will not be compromised?

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I will try to make my answers equally short.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Ng asked what were the mandatory requirements for the preliminary investigation.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But it really depends on the particular circumstances of the death and the context in which it occurs, and whether or not there are particular areas of concern that the Coroner has, which will then drive the steps to be taken in the preliminary investigation.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Ng, Ms Lim and Mr Tan asked about the current process, whether there are safeguards, whether we are doing this because there is a manpower issue, and it is driven entirely by this.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: First of all, I will remind Members what I said at the outset, that we have been doing this for a couple of years now, since the Coroners Act came into force in 2010, using a variety of different steps, technology, video usage, RFID, QR coding.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This then gave us enough confidence to propose this suggestion.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It is not to say that because of this that there will be a flood of non-inspections or non-viewing of the bodies as a result of this.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I think it just gives the Coroner the discretion, on a case-by-case basis, assessing the probative value of each of the different sources of identification, making an overall assessment and deciding whether or not it is sufficiently safe not to actually view the body.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I do not think I will go into the specific steps again.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I think Members can take reference from what I had said earlier.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Ms Lim had asked about the exemption, section 17A.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Ms Lim, to paraphrase her, suggested that there might be circumstances where the request could be motivated by less noble reasons, nefarious reasons, I think, was the phrase that was used.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: If there are suspicious circumstances surrounding a head of state's or a foreign government minister's death in Singapore, then, obviously, it is not in our country's interest to give up on the investigation and to let the foreign state take over the investigations and, in fact, to completely remove the body from Singapore altogether.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, I think that she should be reasonably assuaged.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, all of these steps give us the assurance that the death has not occurred in nefarious or unusual circumstances, and there is enough, sufficient public interest for us to accede to the request.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Tan asked about the rationale of section 17A.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: There are circumstances where a foreign state may have a legitimate interest in the death and request that Singapore does not conduct our post-mortem examination.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: For example, the foreign state may wish to maintain the integrity of the body – I think Ms Lim mentioned "preserve the dignity" – so that it may conduct its own post-mortem examination on its resident or citizen.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: On other occasions, the death may have taken place in Singapore, but the cause of death is really only tangentially connected to Singapore and is instead more closely connected with events and circumstances overseas.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Tan asked whether it is motivated by any particular occasion.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It is really a question of comity, as far as we can to try and accommodate in appropriate situations.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The point here is, at this point in time, the Act does not allow any leeway, whatsoever.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Pillai asked about the Criminal Law (Temporary Provisions) Act or CLTPA.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I understand where Mr Pillai is coming from, when he says that why is there no similar requirement for the Public Prosecutor (PP)'s consent in this case.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Well, first of all, the PP's views, whether or not they are going to be conducting further investigations, its sense of whether there is any impropriety which merits further review or investigation, will all be taken into account.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It is not the same framework as the CLTPA here because in that situation, we are dealing with consent to detain a person.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Here, it is in relation to a request by a foreign party to not conduct a post-mortem here and to release the body to a foreign state.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And, of course, the whole gamut of matters that surround the public interest criteria, including whether or not the PP's view is that there should be a further investigation, will be taken into account.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I would add that the Minister is very unlikely to reach a conclusion that it is in our public interest, where circumstances surrounding the death is either unknown, unclear or it is not apparently the reason, as set out, through a disease or manifest cause and where there might be a suspicion of foul play, then in those situations, in assessing public interest, the Minister will obviously have to consider the PP's position as far as these considerations are concerned.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Ng asked for a clarification of the circumstances in which the Minister's certificate might be revoked.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This minimises the possibility of having to subsequently reconsider similar circumstances, as far as possible.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Obviously, there could be a change in circumstances.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, all of these factors will be taken into account, but for flexibility purposes, there is not a prescribed timeframe in the framework of this Bill for the revocation.
